bermuteo:enwiki:6.title: Bermuda hawk (Generic description and morphological differences from extant hawk species)

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk is listed as extinct by the IUCN with a rough date of 1603.
facts.quote: extinct: 1603

facts.statement: The species Bermuteo avivorus was described by Storrs Lovejoy Olson in 2008.
facts.quote: authority: Olson, 2008

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk was an extinct bird of prey found only on the island of Bermuda.
facts.quote: The Bermuda hawk (Bermuteo avivorus) is an extinct bird of prey that was endemic to Bermuda.

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk was the only species within the genus Bermuteo.
facts.quote: It was the sole member of the genus Bermuteo.

facts.statement: The genus name Bermuteo combines the name of the island Bermuda with the genus Buteo, which contains many hawk and buzzard species.
facts.quote: Bermuteo here is an amalgam of Bermuda and Buteo, an Accipitrid genus which includes various hawk and buzzard species.

facts.statement: The species name avivorus indicates that the bird engaged in catching other birds.
facts.quote: The species name, avivorus, refers to bird-catching behaviour.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains of the Bermuda hawk were found in quaternary deposits on the island of Bermuda.
facts.quote: The Bermuda hawk inhabited the island of Bermuda where the subfossil remains of the species were discovered in quaternary deposits.

facts.statement: The original sample used to describe the species consisted of seven bones from four or five locations, representing at most six individuals.
facts.quote: Olson's sample consisted of seven bones recovered from four or five localities on Bermuda, of which only three were complete (femur, humerus, and tibiotarsi), representing a maximum of just six individuals.

facts.statement: Native evergreen forests of Bermuda cedar and palmetto likely served as habitat for the Bermuda hawk before human settlement.
facts.quote: Prior to human settlement and encroachment, Bermuda was rich in native evergreen forests of Bermuda cedar (Juniperus bermudiana) and palmetto (Sabal bermudana) which may have served as habitat for the species.

facts.statement: Researchers inferred that females of the Bermuda hawk may have been twice as heavy as males.
facts.quote: It was inferred by Olson that the species may have exhibited prominent sexual dimorphism, where the females where potentially twice the mass of the males.

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk likely fed almost exclusively on other birds due to the abundance of endemic bird populations in Bermuda.
facts.quote: Due to the large endemic bird population of Bermuda (a population that would have been far more biodiverse before human settlememt), the hawk likely had little else to feed on than other birds

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk's femur had a uniquely flattened head shape that was smaller and less round than those of other hawk genera.
facts.quote: Unlike other hawk genera, the femur of the Bermuda hawk has a much smaller head that is not as round, exhibiting a flattened, proximodistal shape with the distal margin of the femur's head being near continuous with the posterior crest of the neck.

facts.statement: The distinct wing-like condyle found on the femurs of most Accipitridae birds is reduced in the Bermuda hawk.
facts.quote: He notes also that the "distinct wing-like condyle of the femur in most Accipitridae is reduced in Bermuteo".

facts.statement: Based on bone comparisons, the Bermuda hawk likely ranged in mass from approximately 244g to 495g.
facts.quote: The holotypical femur is most contiguous with that of a small male roadside hawk (Rupornis magnirostris), being just 244-268g (8.6-9oz), while the sample humerus is most comparable to a large female broad-winged hawk (Buteo platypterus) at a maximum mass of 495g (17oz).

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk belongs to the subfamily Buteoninae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Buteoninae

facts.statement: The Bermuda hawk is classified within the family Accipitridae.
facts.quote: Family: Accipitridae

facts.statement: The exact date of extinction is unknown, though 1603 is cited based on explorer sightings.
facts.quote: The exact date of the extinction of the Bermuda hawk is unknown but the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) lists a rough date as 1603, given reason by sightings recorded that year by explorers.

facts.statement: Hunting and the introduction of invasive species like feral pigs in the 17th century likely caused the extinction of the Bermuda hawk.
facts.quote: Its extinction likely followed hunting and the introduction of invasive species to Bermuda in the 17th century, most notably the introduction of feral pigs which have been present on the island as early as 1625.

facts.statement: Deforestation and burning of native forests after European settlement may have contributed to the hawk's extinction.
facts.quote: Large-scale burnings and deforestation of Bermuda's evergreen forests following European settlement also contributed to the rapid alteration of the landscape, and may have contributed to the extinction of the Bermuda hawk.

facts.statement: Historical accounts describe the Bermuda hawk as tame enough to be clubbed by explorers.
facts.quote: A 1603 account by a Diego Ramírez mentions the hawk species and its possible island tameness, stating: "There are many very large dark herons, many very handsome sparrow-hawks, so stupid that we even clubbed them".

facts.statement: Captain John Smith reported a lack of endemic hawks in 1623, suggesting the species had gone extinct by then.
facts.quote: It is highly likley that the species had gone extinct between the settlement of Bermuda in 1612 and 1623, as English explorer and colonial governor Captain John Smith (1579-1631) reported a lack of endemic hawks that year
